title: Trump’s Public Service Announcement: ‘Love Me’
excerpt: The campaign-style ad starts with grainy video footage of President Trump, followed by a clearer look at his red-bathed profile, as his voice promises: “Togethe
body: The campaign-style ad starts with grainy video footage of President Trump, followed by a clearer look at his red-bathed profile, as his voice promises: “Together we will defeat communism, socialism, and Marxism in America.” Then comes the strobe-style rapid display of images of the president

There are plugs for some of his priorities—such as cutting taxes and defending police officers—but one message stays on the screen for fully half of the 30-second commercial: America will never be a communist country
Throughout, an R&B song plays in the background, with falsetto voices singing, over and over: “Love me … Love me … Love me …” At the end comes this: “Paid for by the U.S
Government.” Huh? If the use of taxpayer dollars seems odd—and it should—the explanation that the White House gave me is even more bizarre

No one would say anything with their name attached, but a White House spokesperson told me that the new ad, which began airing this week, is a public service announcement that is “educational and unapologetically patriotic.” A second White House official told me that the ad is “clearly not political,” an assertion that appears intended to provide legal cover
I also received a list of supposedly comparable PSAs from past presidents: George W
Bush spent federal dollars urging the youth of America not to do drugs
Joe Biden had a campaign to encourage the public to get their COVID vaccines
Roosevelt produced radio programs and posters supporting World War II

And now Trump has his own announcement of sorts: “Love me … Love me … Love me …” “These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” the White House spokesperson told me in a statement. [ Read: Trump plans to buy midterm ads about his own record ] The White House would not answer my other questions, including how much money is being spent on these “public service announcements,” which government account is being used to fund them, and who produced the spot
It is unclear how much money the government has spent on these ads and in how many places, but one advertising tracker I spoke with said that it is airing in several major markets
It’s much easier to track such details for political ads because campaigns and other groups are required to file reports with the FCC
The “Love Me” spot aired last night during “Jesse Watters Primetime” on Fox News, and it has also been seen on Newsmax
The ad flashes text in big red letters spelling out Trump’s alleged accomplishments: Largest tax cuts in history , reigniting American manufacturing , and defend law and order and police

At the end, the voice of Dana White, the UFC president, comes on as images of military planes fly overhead. “He is the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met and nothing is going to stop him from fighting so hard for the country that he loves,” White says
A shorter version of the ad appeared on the White House’s official YouTube page nearly two weeks ago

Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a Republican, compared the ad to something that a far-right former Hungarian prime minister would attempt. “It’s not like they need a GoFundMe page to have the dollars to do that sort of ad, and they could do it,” he told reporters. “But using taxpayer dollars, it feels like Viktor Orbán.” Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said that the ad appeared to violate federal law. “It is blatantly unethical under numerous federal ethics provisions proscribing the use of government resources for political campaigns,” he wrote on social media

Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, who is poised to become the top Democrat on a key oversight committee, sent a letter today to Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, with detailed questions about the cost, source of funds, and legal basis for the spot. “The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds,” she wrote

Top Democratic appropriators also wrote to demand the ad be taken down immediately: “This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America.” Donald Sherman, the president of the watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, told me it’s “certainly odd” and unlike anything he has seen before. “It goes out of its way, it seems, to look and feel like propaganda as opposed to something more substantive,” he said. [ Read: The watchdogs are barking themselves hoarse ] Sherman said the ad likely does not violate the Hatch Act, which limits political activities for executive branch employees but exempts the president

It more likely breaches federal appropriations laws, Sherman said, that restrict federal agencies from using taxpayer money for “publicity or propaganda.” Any enforcement would come from the Government Accountability Office, which operates at the request of congressional committees that are presently controlled by Republicans

A GAO spokesperson told me late this afternoon the office had not received any requests for decisions on the matter. “That’s the rub!” Sherman said. “This video is directed at benefiting the current majority in Congress, and the current majority in Congress has repeatedly refrained from reining in the current president’s corruption and behavior

I’m not holding my breath for them to do anything about it.” Although I received few answers from the White House, I did receive some from JMSN, pronounced “Jameson,” the Albanian American artist behind the song used in the ad

He said in an emailed statement that he did not authorize the use of his music, which has become a popular soundtrack on social media for users editing together their own photos. “I am looking for a lawyer now in order to see what our options are and how to proceed,” he said. “I have never been in this situation before, so need help in navigating something of this magnitude.”

title: Trump Should Stop Hosting Summits
excerpt: State visits are a normal and necessary part of diplomacy
body: State visits are a normal and necessary part of diplomacy
National leaders should, from time to time, sit with one another in person and have candid conversations
Summit meetings between the American president and his counterparts from Moscow and Beijing are particularly tricky because of the innately tense relationship between two adversaries

Food and hospitality are part of the festivities, but in the end, such summits provide important human contact at the highest level, and as a result, crucial business can get done that might not be possible over a telephone or in messages delivered through ambassadors
At least, that’s how these visits are supposed to work

In the Donald Trump White House, summits are hazardous excursions during which the interests of the United States are shoved aside by a president whose cringe-inducing admiration of dictators makes these meetings into rituals of American humiliation
The country would be better off if Trump just stopped hosting or attending them
Summits are a problem in this administration for two reasons
Most important, Trump’s unpredictability and obvious lack of preparation make them dangerous
State visits require a lot of political groundwork, and leaders rarely go into top-level meetings without a set of issues they’ve already agreed to discuss
This agenda-setting gets done long before a president actually sits down with another head of state so that stray asides (or rising tempers) do not derail whatever business needs to be discussed
The grim outcomes of previous summits with Trump, however, suggest that they are seat-of-the-pants affairs, with little preparation, or perhaps with preparation that was ignored by the president

Some of them, such as Trump’s previous meetings with Xi Jinping, have been brief talks alongside overseas events (such as at the G20 summits during his first term) when Trump improvised efforts to mitigate the damage from his needless trade wars

And some of them, such as his meetings with the North Korean strongman Kim Jong Un and the Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, have been fiascoes. [ Read: Xi is getting what he wants ] These summits with dictators produced outcomes that were worse than nothing, in part because Trump is so susceptible to pomp and flattery

After seizing the dubious honor of being the first American sitting president to visit North Korea, Trump returned and glowed about how he “fell in love” with the young menace running that prison state

Kim probably thought it had gone well too; he has since been able to build up his nuclear arsenal while watching Trump go to war with Iran over a nuclear program that has not yet produced a single weapon
Trump even admitted last summer that his nuclear-armed friend in Pyongyang will be “fine” as long as America has “a smart president” such as him
No one, however, has taken Trump to the cleaners more times than Putin
Trump seems to both venerate and fear the Kremlin leader, and when they are left in a room together, things do not go well for the United States
After their 2018 meeting in Helsinki, Trump stood next to Putin and told the world that he accepted the word of a former KGB spy over reports from the U.S. intelligence community
And this was at a time when the president had a Cabinet and staff far more willing to tell him hard truths than his current circle of sycophants
When Trump met Putin in Alaska in 2025—well, let’s stop right there for a moment
The President went to Alaska to meet a Russian leader , rather than hosting him at the White House or meeting him in a third country

This location allowed Putin to fly in and drag Trump in front of the cameras to force him to listen to Putin reiterate Russia’s brutal stance on Ukraine, and then—adding a true insult—Putin turned down the nice lunch Trump offered so that he could hop back over to Russia
Both men barely had time for a cup of coffee
What Trump said to his Russian counterpart we may never know, but this was worse than not meeting at all: Trump looked weak and hapless, while Putin looked determined and in control
And that’s another reason to call off these summits while Trump is in office: They are humiliating in almost every respect
They make the United States look like a supplicant instead of a superpower, and they showcase the president’s unstable personality
Like Putin before him, Xi got the red-carpet treatment on his arrival at Joint Base Andrews yesterday
This is an honor, as my colleague Jonathan Lemire noted this morning , that American presidents usually reserve only for the Pope
But Xi got an honor guard and a military flyover

Trump, who insists on saluting during the national anthem instead of placing his hand over his heart as is traditional, looked up and visibly winced at the sound of the jet overhead, while Xi, who seemed largely bored with the whole business, didn’t flinch. (Trump, for some reason, also wore a long overcoat and gloves on a seasonable day with temperatures in the mid-60s.) The optics of meeting the leader of the world’s largest autocracy on a red carpet was bad enough, but then Trump did another thing that can be a problem at such moments: He decided to speak off the cuff

The president of the United States reportedly joked to the Chinese autocrat about how the Chinese press corps had the “friendliest” reporters—this, on a day when American reporters were fighting with Trump in court over their right to enter the White House
Once at the White House, Trump took Xi for a quick tour
Trump had long ago replaced Joe Biden’s portrait in the hall of presidents with a picture of an autopen, a petty jab from a small and petty man, and on their walk, he made sure that Xi saw it

He even gave the Chinese leader a bit of a pat on the arm while yukking it up. [ Read: The deferential president ] This was too much even for the conservative writer Charles Cooke of National Review , who posted on X about Trump’s “grotesque behavior.” Xi, Cooke said, “is a communist dictator, and the head of a foreign state
Our internal divisions are not fair game in this context.” But Trump does not think in these terms

His summits are a national hazard precisely because Trump apparently does not understand that he is representing the United States; instead, he seems to think he’s just having a visit with some of the guys in a very cool club of which he’d very much like to be a member
His attempts to ingratiate himself are obvious and pathetic, and they function as a giant tell to America’s opponents: This president likes you, fears you, and wants your approval
These summits can have serious ramifications

title: The Doomed Midterm Strategy Some Republicans Are Trying
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
With the midterm elections just 40 days away, Republicans are running hard—many of them away from President Trump

Representative Maria Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican whose district Trump won by 15 points in 2024, recently released an ad critiquing the administration’s immigration enforcement, saying that Hispanic voters feel “betrayed.” Byron Donalds, the GOP’s nominee for governor of Florida, scrubbed most references to Trump from his website—a notable move considering that the foundation of Donalds’s entire career has been fidelity to the Donald
The Senate contenders Mike Rogers of Michigan and Ashley Hinson of Iowa are both calling for an end to the Iran war
Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor of Wisconsin, has even suddenly changed his mind and now believes that Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election
The number of prominent Republicans distancing themselves from Trump has accelerated, or at least reached a critical mass, in the past 10 days

The shift is interesting—first, as an indication of what information GOP candidates are receiving privately about the president’s unpopularity and its drag on them, and second, because public critiques of Trump from Republicans have been vanishingly rare, no matter how unwise, outrageous, or unpopular his actions have been
But the defections are perhaps better understood as a sign of normalcy, even in a deeply abnormal context
A president’s party almost always loses seats in a midterm, a result of the pendulum effect in elections
And the dynamics of this race are especially challenging for Republicans because Trump is historically unpopular , outpacing even his own poor ratings in 2018, when Democrats dominated the midterms
Trump is now presiding over persistent inflation, exacerbated by a failing war of choice in Iran
All of this predicts that GOP candidates would be wary of Trump
News coverage about members of a president’s party trying to run away from him appears like a brood of cicadas, in this case popping up nearly every four years
You can easily find clips about Democrats trying to disassociate themselves from Bill Clinton in 1994, Republicans recoiling from George W

Bush in 2006, and Democrats avoiding Barack Obama four years after that, then again in 2014 . (The 1998 and 2002 midterms were atypical because of the Clinton impeachment and a post-9/11 boost for Bush, respectively.) Though it’s mostly forgotten now, some Republicans tried to separate themselves from Trump in 2018, too, despite his effort to make the election about him. (“ Pretend I’m on the ballot ,” he told voters

After the voting, he blamed Republican losses on the defectors .) Watching endangered officeholders try to run away from their party’s president every four years reminds me of a moment in Arrested Development in which a couple considers an open marriage
Lindsay asks whether it ever fixes a relationship. “No

It never does,” her husband, Tobias, replies. “These people somehow delude themselves into thinking it might, but … but it might work for us.” In a few isolated, marginal cases, a candidate successfully manages to separate themselves from the unpopular president and his party

In 2010, the Democratic Senate candidate Joe Manchin of West Virginia recorded an ad in which he fired a rifle at an Obama-backed carbon bill and won, but Manchin had years of credibility as a centrist governor to draw on
In aggregate, however, these efforts don’t work: The usual pattern is that a president’s party loses seats

Because hard-core partisans are more likely to represent safe seats , they are also more likely to survive big midterm waves, whereas many moderates who distance themselves from the president lose because they are more likely to occupy contested seats

One reason that so few Republican officeholders have spoken out against Trump during the past eight years is that even the ones who were willing to criticize Trump lost their seats in 2018—their attempts at distancing weren’t enough to overcome the voter backlash against Trump
Sometimes, the in-party loses seats for reasons largely beyond their control, such as big macroeconomic currents
But some of the specific cases where Republicans are breaking with Trump are on issues where the GOP as a whole is aligned with the president
If the party retains congressional control, a few scattered critics won’t be able to change the consensus
Hinson may be sincere in her desire to end the war in Iran—though her repeated votes against reining it in, including one just last week, raise doubts

Regardless, voters have no reason to believe that giving Republicans another two years of control of Congress would help end the war, given that the GOP House and Senate leaders have tried to sidestep resolutions calling for an end to the war and have opposed any actual restrictions on the White House
Or consider Salazar’s shot across Trump’s bow on immigration

The idea that Trump is going to walk away from strict immigration enforcement, his signature issue for a decade and one dear to his base, is absurd, and House Republicans as a whole have shown no interest in restraining him

Salazar said on Face the Nation this past weekend that Trump was “very receptive” to her message, but Trump himself told reporters, “I’m very strong on the borders, and she isn’t.” The mystery is whether Salazar is gullible or just hopes that her voters are
Many things about this moment in American history are unsettling and novel, and Trump’s threats to disrupt the elections themselves continue to cast a shadow over the midterms
But watching old patterns repeat is a reminder of how normal the dynamics of this campaign have been
Nearly every indication is that Democrats will win control of the House; the real questions are how large their victory will be and whether they can gain control of the Senate as well
In this environment, many Republicans can’t do much to save themselves
But because Trump is likely to blame losing candidates after the election anyway, rather than examine his own role, they don’t have many reasons to hold their criticism

title: Why Female Fans Can’t Win
excerpt: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
body: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present

As far as journalism assignments go, Margaret Pratt Allen was handed a fun one: Investigate whether women can be sports fans. “For two years the New York World gave me costly tickets to the season’s major sporting events so that I might observe and report whether or not women were there, and what seemed to be their reactions and interest,” she recounted in the May 1928 issue of The Atlantic . “I saw the Yankees and the Giants clash for the pennant, and I watched Firpo knock Dempsey into the press box and Dempsey knock Firpo into oblivion (at least I had a $27.50 ringside seat from which I was supposed to see this), not to mention other less thrilling affairs.” (The latter refers to the infamous heavyweight championship fight between Jack Dempsey and Luis Ángel Firpo in 1923—adjusted for inflation, Pratt Allen’s ticket would’ve cost more than $500 today.) Sports fanaticism was on the rise in America in the 1920s, when superstar athletes (ever heard of Babe Ruth?) drew crowds of tens of thousands of both sexes, across a variety of sports
Pratt Allen acknowledged herself to be “a pretty good baseball fan as women go,” eager to applaud a good play and posssessing extensive knowledge of the sport rivaling that of her male companions
Nevertheless, her Atlantic story on women and athletics was constrained by the gendered assumptions of her time
Women had begun to compete in the modern Olympic Games only at the turn of the century, initially limited to more “ refined ” activities, such as tennis, croquet, and golf
And when they did show rousing enthusiasm watching games, they were criticized for their behavior

Hoping that women’s presence could temper the boisterous behavior of male attendees, and aware that women too wanted to spectate and spend money at games, some baseball teams started regularly hosting “ Ladies’ Days ,” offering them free or cheap entry (though in some cases they were required to be accompanied by a man)
As these promotions took off, so did complaints about the female fans: that they cheered “ at the wrong times ,” that their presence caused more disruption than it kept in check

Pratt Allen disagreed, but in the form of a backhanded compliment. “The stuff that fans are made of—frenzied, hysterical, pleading, shouting, swearing fans—is not of the same piece as the pattern from which women are cut,” she wrote
At the Dempsey-Firpo boxing match, women were “conspicuous by their absence or their uncomprehending blankness in the face of the mob frenzy which gripped the male fans,” she explained

And women would never become so caught up in the game as to lob things from the stands: “Plenty of men would sacrifice brand-new headgear to the greatness of the moment, but can you imagine a ball game meaning more to a woman than a hat?” Sure, they “go because it’s the thing, these days, to be interested in all sport,” but ultimately, as the headline declared, “Women Aren’t Fans.” Pratt Allen’s essay nods at the perennial bind women find themselves in: Damned if they cheer; damned if they don’t
Even if a female spectator “was just terribly glad St
Louis had won, her grown-up self, her real woman self” would keep her jubilance in check, Pratt Allen explained
And when women and girls have engaged in unrestrained fangirl behavior, they have been routinely mocked and denigrated for their joy

In 1964, one writer called Beatles fans “who scream themselves into hysteria” “the least fortunate of their generation.” In 2012, a critic referred to a One Direction album as “a reliable shriek inducer in girls who have not yet decided that shrieking doesn’t become them.” Modern fandom in particular has turned Pratt Allen’s assertion about “the stuff that fans are made of” on its head
The fangirl familiar to us today— shouting herself hoarse for the likes of Taylor Swift or BTS—might indeed be “frenzied, hysterical, pleading,” in Pratt Allen’s eyes
What is a girl to do? In other words, the question is not whether women can be fans, but whether they are seen as the right kind of fan
The behavior of the female spectator ringside, courtside, in the stands, or in the gallery has long confounded those observing them
And here is where I come clean as a fangirl myself
I have screamed with abandon at concerts, but I have also held back, wondering if such enthusiasm befits a professional woman in her 30s with a mortgage and a baby
But what remains unclear is how a woman can ever be a fan in the way that she wants to be—without judgment not only from others, but also from herself.

title: Another Female Democrat Is Mean, Apparently
excerpt: In February 2024, according to a former staff member who told the story to The New York Times , Representative Mary Peltola , an Alaska Democrat running for the
body: In February 2024, according to a former staff member who told the story to The New York Times , Representative Mary Peltola , an Alaska Democrat running for the Senate, pushed an aide

As the Times put it in a report published yesterday, Peltola “shoved a male employee in the chest with one hand, causing him to stumble backward.” You might wonder why the paper of record is reporting this detail
Did the employee then tumble off a cliff and die? The Times does not mention any bodily harm, beyond the backward stumble
The encounter is instead offered as evidence of what the Times calls “a campaign and congressional office marked by chaos.” Chaos
The attempted exposé of Peltola is the latest installment in a familiar genre
Democratic staffers (they are almost always Democrats) complain off the record about the private behavior of their boss, who is almost always female, toward them
The behavior in question ranges from inappropriate to, more often, somewhat inappropriate to completely appropriate
One notorious example concerns former Representative Katie Porter of California, who shouted, as she was being filmed, “Get out of my fucking shot,” at a staffer

Although nobody enjoys being shouted at, there is a certain urgency about getting the staff out of a camera shot that is supposed to focus exclusively on the principal. [ Marc Novicoff: Democrats’ great Alaskan hope ] The classic of the genre involves Senator Amy Klobuchar, who was deemed abusive by staffers in 2019, as she was mounting a presidential campaign, for episodes such as berating them for bringing her a salad on a plane without including a fork
Klobuchar was reduced to eating her salad with a comb
The story was supposed to make Klobuchar look unreasonable, if not crazy
To my mind, it reflected poorly on the staffer who did not think to procure the fork
The Times ’ Peltola exposé labels the shove as “one of the more notable incidents described by former aides.” This raises the intriguing question of what the less notable incidents entail
In one episode recounted by the Times , Peltola grew frustrated with a prep session for interactions with the news media

The story gravely notes that Peltola “picked up a water bottle and pretended it was a microphone, shoving it toward a staff member as she berated her.” The bottle did not strike the target, but it reportedly came within an inch of doing so, according to “text messages sent at the time.” One can only imagine the carnage Peltola narrowly averted. (Two other people present at the time described the exchange as “lighthearted.”) Peltola’s reign of terror includes text messages requesting more campaign signs

In pursuit of this goal, which seems quite reasonable, she reportedly texted, “BIG SIGNS NEED TO BE SENT TO SOUTHEAST,” and, “OUR SIGN GAME IS FUCKED.” Peltola also wrote disparagingly about a progressive organization. “I hope Planned Parenthood knows that if we don’t win it’s more their loss than ours
FUCK THOSE BITCHES,” she texted her staff in January 2024, according to the Times , which published an image of the text
And, apparently referring specifically to one Planned Parenthood board member, Peltola later wrote, “I hope she dies of a botched abortion.” This was an obvious, if hostile, joke
The anecdote suggests that the staffers are aggrieved by Peltola’s political leanings as well as her managerial failings
The centerpiece of the story revolves around the care and feeding of Meatball, the office lizard

The Times presents this piece of the puzzle in the tone of Watergate-style disclosures, complete with details about sourcing: “Meatball’s preferred diet consisted of live crickets, according to three staff members familiar with the demand, including two who fed the chameleon.” You can almost imagine Ben Bradlee inspecting the copy and asking skeptically why the third source was not directly involved in the cricket-feeding. (I don’t know the answer

I was not in the parking garage where this anecdote was presumably shared.) The Times elaborates upon the indignities this task entails: “On at least one occasion, the crickets escaped in the office and had to be recaptured, according to two former aides who witnessed it as well as a photo viewed by The Times that showed aides in the office trying to trap the crickets using manila folders and small paper cups.” A naive reader might conclude that this episode is harmless farce, or perhaps reflects haplessness on the part of the staff

Did the crickets get loose through some elaborate Escape From Alcatraz plot, or did the staffers simply fumble the job? (One suspects the latter.) The Times explains that, to her staffers, this task “exemplified the disregard Ms

Peltola appeared to have for her employees.” Was Peltola supposed to feed Meatball herself? This expectation would seem to make poor use of her comparative skill advantage, not to mention burden her with a frequently impossible task, given her need to travel between Washington, D.C., and Alaska
The story does contain one bona fide example of improper behavior—an allegation that she sometimes used the slur faggot
Four former staff members report directly hearing her use the word
If true, it certainly reflects poorly on her

The Peltola campaign denied that she’d used the slur. [ Mark Leibovich: The Democrats aren’t built for this ] Yet the overall impression the story conveys is not an office beset by chaos, but one rife with staffers burdened with unrealistic expectations of workplace norms
Berating subordinates is a poor management practice
But it does not constitute chaos or the level of abuse that would justify a national news story

The fact that staffers for Peltola as well as for other Democratic politicians apparently categorize being scolded by their boss as a level of scandal requiring them to alert the media reflects a solipsistic tendency
Staffers working for Democrats—but not for Republicans—now commonly use the national media as their human-resources department
They also use the media to publicly denounce their boss over matters of policy
Democratic staffers have sent letters demanding action on impeachment , climate change , and, on multiple occasions , the Middle East, among other issues
Democratic staffers like these seem to believe that their role is to serve as a kind of moral check on their boss, to issue public dissents when a politician fails to uphold their preferred stances
If that is the position they imagine for themselves, then they probably take umbrage at being asked to feed her lizard
The question is whether that kind of behavior is worth going—anonymously—to The New York Times
More important, these Democrats should come to terms with the reality that sometimes, when you work for a busy, prominent person in a high-stress environment, your job really is to feed the lizard.

title: Why Fauda Is So Popular in the Arab World
excerpt: Before this week, I’d never watched an episode of Fauda , the Israeli-made, Netflix-distributed counterterrorism thriller
body: Before this week, I’d never watched an episode of Fauda , the Israeli-made, Netflix-distributed counterterrorism thriller
The show stars Lior Raz as Doron Kabilio, an undercover Israeli mista’arvim (Arabic-speaking) operative who over the course of the show infiltrates various Hamas and Hezbollah cells
What drew me to binge all 59 episodes in less than a week was the news that the show had catapulted into Netflix’s Top 10 across a range of Arab countries
In the second week of September, it was the No. 1 show in Lebanon, No. 4 in both Jordan and Qatar, No. 5 in the United Arab Emirates, and No. 9 in Kuwait
For any Israeli drama—much less one about undercover operatives apprehending (and often killing) Palestinian and Lebanese militants—to become a hit across the Arab world is remarkable
For it to happen in a season partially devoted to the events of October 7, 2023, and their aftermath is nothing short of astonishing
Cross-pollination between Israel and the Arab world has been limited ever since Israel’s independence in 1948, with only six out of the 22 Arab states even recognizing Israel’s existence as a state

But although negative tropes and stereotypes about Israelis and Jews have been commonplace for decades across the Arab world, that doesn’t necessarily preclude people having a human interest in seeing the other side, or hearing its side of the story

Fauda is also a show with a large and diverse cast of multifaceted Palestinian characters, with their own dilemmas, backstories, and motivations. [ Read: Watching Israeli TV’s Fauda as a Palestinian ] What I took away from the early seasons was a sense of sorrow at the circumstances of life for Israelis and Palestinians, dwelling amid the chaos
I’m Palestinian myself; my father was one of 10 siblings from a rural village in the West Bank
But I always hoped for peace, and for a solution that could end the military rule in the West Bank and give people on both sides a chance at a more peaceful life

I lived through and witnessed the repeated failures of peace processes in the 2000s, and the gradual deterioration of relations—and loss of hope for peace—in the 2010s that ultimately led to October 7
Fauda dramatizes this spiral in a compelling way

It shows people on both sides—often spurred by their grief, fear, or hunger for revenge—convinced that one more operation or one more act of violence is the answer, only to create the next impetus of grievance driving the next round of revenge
Violence in this story rarely settles an old score without simultaneously creating a new one
Doron’s unassailable plot armor allows him to bounce from chaotic event to chaotic event

Where Hamlet’s fatal flaw was indecision, and Macbeth’s fatal flaw was “vaulting ambition,” Doron’s flaw (albeit not one that has yet proved fatal) is simply a tendency to keep riding on his instincts
I read this, at least in part, as a critique of the Israeli political direction of the 2010s and early 2020s
Israel survived many wars and intifadas, and emerged stronger
This may have stoked the delusion that the conflict, rather than needing to be resolved, could simply be contained
But trying to contain the conflict would not work

In April 2014, when Fauda was being developed, one of its co-creators, Avi Issacharoff, was expressing such fears: writing in The Times of Israel about the faltering Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations, arguing that both sides had an interest in keeping peace talks alive, and warning that the two sides might be “headed toward conflict” if not

One of the most memorable moments in the show comes in the first season, when Abu Ahmad, a Hamas commander who is that season’s major antagonist, seemingly anticipates Hamas’s real-life logic behind the October 7 attack
He plans to unleash a sarin-gas attack in a synagogue, intending to provoke Israel into an overreaction that might cause a wider Middle Eastern war that could threaten Israel’s existence
He says: “The Jews will respond with an extremely severe retaliation

They’ll be committing such unprecedented war crimes that all Islamic states will intervene, including Iran.” Abu Ahmad is ultimately taken down by his own young protégé, Walid, who discovers that Doron has penetrated the organization under an assumed identity
The proposed sarin attack never takes place

Across the next three seasons—as the counterpunching between Israel and the Islamist Palestinian groups continues—Doron gets sucked back into espionage again and again, in storylines that can feel eerily contemporary, including the kidnapping of Israeli hostages and the kidnapping of Doron’s family members
In real life, the strategic logic that Abu Ahmad describes in Season 1 is not far removed from what Hamas’s leadership appears to have contemplated before October 7
Hamas documents captured in Gaza show that Yahya Sinwar hoped a spectacular attack on Israel would invite a devastating Israeli response in Gaza and ignite a much broader confrontation
The October 7 attack did not quite produce the regional uprising that Hamas appears to have hoped for
Hamas killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages
The subsequent war in Gaza left more than 71,000 Palestinians dead, according to Gaza health-authority figures accepted by the Israel Defense Forces, including thousands of combatants
The majority of the housing and infrastructure in Gaza has been destroyed, displacing most of Gaza’s roughly 2.1 million people
The conflict spread, as Hezbollah attacked from Lebanon, the Houthis joined in from Yemen, and, eventually, Iran launched direct exchanges of fire with Israel—just as Abu Ahmad had hoped

Equally consequentially, images of the war in Gaza generated mass protests abroad, disputes between Israel and allied governments—including the United Kingdom, France, and Canada—and a fierce international argument over the proportionality of Israel’s campaign
Today, for the first time in history, polling suggests that more Americans sympathize with Palestinians than with Israelis
That is the world into which Fauda ’s fifth season arrives
The chaos escaped all of the boundaries that had previously contained it
For one thing, it starts in 2025, and depicts October 7 in a two-episode flashback

title: The Download: a bid to scrap the virtual wall and AI hits Climate Week
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

A congressional representative just proposed killing America’s border tower program Delia Ramirez, a Democratic US representative from Illinois, has announced plans to introduce legislation to terminate the surveillance tower program along the country’s southern border
The announcement comes just days after publication of an MIT Technology Review investigation, “Dying on Camera,” which looked at deaths near these towers
Nearly one in four deaths we analyzed between 2015 and early 2026 occurred within their advertised range

Ramirez, who sits on the Homeland Security Committee, cited our reporting that nearly “1,100 people have died within range of a billion-dollar surveillance tower system between 2015 and 2026,” adding, “The towers that we have paid a billion dollars to just don’t work.” Here’s what she’s proposing and what it could mean for the border surveillance program . —Eileen Guo Read all of MIT Technology Review’s groundbreaking “virtual wall” investigation here

Roundtables: the deadly failures of the virtual border wall The US spent billions building the “virtual wall” of surveillance towers along its southern border, promising they will help detect and apprehend border crossers and save lives
But MIT Technology Review has documented more than a thousand people who moved through areas watched by these towers without being caught—and ultimately died there

Next Monday, join our editor-in-chief Mat Honan, senior AI reporter James O’Donnell, and senior reporter for features and investigations Eileen Guo for a subscriber-only conversation about the investigation
They’ll examine the failures of border surveillance technology and uncover the stories of the people who die in the borderlands
Register now to attend on Monday, September 28 at 19:00 BST / 2:00pm EDT / 11:00am PDT
Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables
AI is dominating the conversation at Climate Week —Casey Crownhart AI is the unavoidable topic at this year’s New York Climate Week, with tension growing over its costs and benefits
The technology is attracting more attention and money to energy technologies, some of which are low- or zero-emission
But the data center buildout has come with a hefty environmental toll, and a whole lot of natural gas is coming online to meet the demand
Overall, what I’m hearing this week is that many in the climate sector are skeptical of AI, at best
This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter
Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday

The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 An OpenAI agent has executed the first known AI hack of a government site It breached an Australian government health data portal in June. ( CNN ) + OpenAI notified Australia three months later through a public mailbox. ( BBC ) + No patient records are believed to have been accessed. ( Guardian ) + Its agents also tried to breach three other sites. ( NYT $) + Here’s why AI agents cheat to reach their goals. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Data stolen in the FBI hack exposes agents’ sensitive intelligence roles It identifies staff working on China, Russia, and cyber. ( Reuters $) + And may have exposed the FBI’s own hacking unit. ( 404 Media ) + The group behind the incident claims it isn’t financially motivated. ( Register ) 3 The US rejected calls from OpenAI and Anthropic for global AI standards A Trump advisor said global rules threatened the country’s AI lead. ( BBC ) + America’s AI leaders had urged the UN to coordinate on safety. ( Gizmodo ) + The AI industry has taken a doomer turn. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Meta has unveiled new AI glasses—and a pendant for Muse Camera-free smart glasses address growing privacy concerns. ( Verge ) + While the Muse Charm enables hands-free interaction with the AI agent. ( BBC ) + Mark Zuckerberg wants Muse to be a “personal superintelligence.” ( Axios ) + Meta also showed off new VR glasses. ( CNBC ) 5 China is accelerating its AI push ahead of the Xi-Trump summit Huawei and Alibaba have both unveiled new flagship chips. ( CNBC ) + The country’s AI industry has shrugged off America’s safety panic. ( Atlantic $) + The US leads in AI models, but China has talent and political edges. ( NYT $) + Chinese models have divided the White House. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 US lawmakers have proposed new rules for blocking Chinese tech The bipartisan bill would require broader review of national security risks. ( Hill ) + And give Congress the power to overturn FCC bans. ( Reuters $) 7 Tech giants have urged Trump to withdraw $103,265 H-1B fee They say the charge could weaken US competitiveness. ( WSJ $) 8 Scientists have detected radio signals from an exoplanet for the first time The signals likely come from intense magnetic activity on the planet. ( Wired $) 9 An invisible force has a mysterious effect on aging Shielding fruit flies from Earth’s magnetic field changed their lifespans. ( 404 Media ) 10 ‘Dopamine sites’ are recreating the thrill of shopping without paying FoodNeverComes has attracted more than 2.7 million visitors since June. ( BBC ) Quote of the day “They decided to break the law.” —Ed Santow, co-founder of the Human Technology Institute, tells ABC radio why there should be serious legal consequences for OpenAI agents hacking Australia’s Medicare statistics portal
One more thing The quest to figure out farming on Mars If ever a blade of grass grew on Mars, those days are over
But could they begin again? What would it take to grow plants to feed future astronauts on Mars?  To grow food there, we can’t just drop seeds in the ground and add water
We will need to create a layer of soil that can support life
And to do that, we first have to get rid of the red planet’s toxic salts.  Researchers recently discovered a potential solution—and the early signs are promising

Brown We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + Meet Alfie, a dog with flowing locks that croons like an opera singer . + Watch the 100 wildest homemade plane flights and crashes from Red Bull Flugtag. + Marmot researchers have launched OnlyMarms , a free, G-rated account of cute videos that funds their work through tips. + The full trailer for Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary is here, and somehow it looks even weirder than expected.

title: AI is dominating the conversation at Climate Week
excerpt: AI is the unavoidable topic at Climate Week: With world leaders and climate advocates packed into Manhattan, one question keeps surfacing: will AI help solve th
body: AI is the unavoidable topic at Climate Week: With world leaders and climate advocates packed into Manhattan, one question keeps surfacing: will AI help solve the climate crisis, or make it worse? Money is flowing, but unevenly: Climate-tech VC investment hit $26 billion in early 2026—up 55%—but much of it is chasing data center products, leaving carbon removal and low-carbon fuels starved of funding
Big Tech's emissions are already rising: Microsoft, Google, and Meta all once had bold climate pledges
Now all three have seen emissions climb, driven largely by the energy demands of AI infrastructure

Public patience is wearing thin: Communities near data centers are pushing back over pollution and noise, and the UN's climate chief warned that tech companies need to prove AI's benefits outweigh its costs. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145048" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> This week, world leaders descended on Manhattan for the UN General Assembly
It’s also New York Climate Week—investors, policymakers, advocates, and journalists are colliding at panels, talks, and fancy dinners
With so many climate voices in one place, the discourse can feel a little louder than usual
This year, the unavoidable topic is artificial intelligence
There’s been a growing tension bubbling up about AI’s impacts on climate and climate tech
Depending on where you stand, you might point to AI’s potential for advancing research, or to the way funding and attention from Big Tech is trickling into energy startups
Or you might focus on the emissions-heavy natural-gas buildout that’s unfolding to meet the sector’s electricity demand
Everyone seems to agree that AI is important
The big question for those in the climate world, and the conversation I’m constantly having and hearing this week, involves how you see its influence unfolding

UN Secretary-General António Guterres highlighted the AI and climate crossover in a speech on the first day of the assembly. “The climate crisis fuels instability and displacement,” Guterres said. “Artificial intelligence could help solve all these challenges, or it could make them worse.” It feels relevant that this year is the first that the world has really had to grapple with the fact that climate goals are slipping out of reach
A recent report from the UN Environment Program said that the world has nearly passed the point where we could possibly keep warming to less than 1.5 °C above preindustrial levels

Since we’ve essentially missed this target, the report lays out the need not only to quickly and drastically reduce greenhouse-gas emissions, but also to employ carbon removal to help suck up emissions that have already been released into the atmosphere

The billion-dollar question is whether AI could help with any of this.  The energy-intensive technology is certainly shining a spotlight on the need to build out electricity supplies and shore up grid reliability
The result is more attention and money for energy technologies, some of which happen to be low- or zero-emissions
As I’ve covered before, startups across the energy and climate sectors are benefiting
Firms in nuclear, geothermal, wind, and solar power have signed deals with the likes of Google, Meta, and others looking to power their new or growing data centers
Global climate-tech investment from venture capital hit $26 billion in the first half of 2026, according to data from Currence, a finance tracker for the industry
That’s 55% higher than last year, and products and services for data centers are getting a massive slice of that pie
But as a Semafor piece about the report points out, some sectors are slipping through the cracks: Carbon management and low-carbon fuels saw VC investment plummet this year
These are important solutions for addressing climate change but may not be able to sell themselves to a data center
So far, the data center buildout has come with a hefty emissions toll
A few years ago, Microsoft, Google, and Meta all had ambitious goals to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions
Now they’ve all seen emissions rise, largely because of data centers that are needed to power AI
AI could help speed up progress in areas like the search for new catalysts, as Evelyn Wang, MIT’s VP of energy and climate, pointed out duri n g a panel

And data centers won’t add to climate and water problems forever, Wang told the Associated Press . (She puts the timeline at about a decade until data centers no longer add to planet-warming emissions.) But a whole lot of natural gas is coming online to meet the immediate demand created by new data centers

And once those power plants are built, they have a decades-long lifetime.  That’s partly why public pushback to AI is growing—people are seeing more pollution and noise near these data centers and the power plants that provide them with electricity

Overall, what I’m hearing this week is that many in the climate sector are skeptical of AI, at best.  “AI leaders are now on thin ice when it comes to license to operate and sinking deep underwater when it comes to public support,” said UN climate chief Simon Stiell in a speech this week. “Tech titans need to start showing why the benefits of AI outweigh its skyrocketing costs—for the many, not just the tiny few.”  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter
To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

title: How due process, not the First Amendment, got the White House ban on reporters blocked in court
url:
<title>How due process, not the First Amendment, got the White House ban on reporters blocked in court</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761830/original/file-20260923-50-ljypgi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Reporter Akayla Gardner reports near the White House after being denied entry following President Donald Trump&#39;s ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico, Sept. 19, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Trump%20News%20Media/6db06ecca7e947faaef5f9149f028154/photo">AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/24/politics/trump-press-lawsuit-ruling-white-house-access">temporarily restore journalists’ access</a> to the White House on Sept. 24, 2026. As he had in a <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2018/11/16/media/cnn-trump-lawsuit-hearing/index.html">similar case in 2018</a>, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly decided the revocation of the reporters’ press passes likely violated their Fifth Amendment right to due process. </p>

<p>His decision comes just days after President Donald Trump <a href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-ban-ms-now-media-cnn-politico-72f9acf68244ca70e9078d9d3661c722">revoked credentials</a> from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, citing “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”</p>

<p>On social media, Trump posted, “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES <a href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/117293599348325006">when they’re covering the President</a>.”</p>

<p><a href="https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/post/a-roundup-of-donald-trump-actions-against-the-press/">This was not Trump’s first attempt</a> at banning journalists from the White House. <a href="https://www.npr.org/2018/11/13/667425530/cnn-sues-trump-administration-over-jim-acostas-press-credentials">During his first term</a>, he sought to ban CNN’s Jim Acosta by revoking his credentials <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2018/11/13/business/media/cnn-jim-acosta-trump-lawsuit.html">following a contentious news conference</a> about the 2018 midterm elections. </p>

<p>In that conflict, CNN filed a lawsuit, arguing that, “If left unchallenged, the actions of the White House would create a dangerous chilling effect for <a href="https://www.politico.com/story/2018/11/13/cnn-sues-trump-administration-985747">any journalist who covers our elected officials</a>.”</p>

<p>Journalism organizations also responded. The Committee to Protect Journalists, the Radio Television Digital News Association and even Acosta’s peers at The Daily Caller – a right-leaning news outlet – <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2018/11/08/media/trump-acosta-press-pass-reaction/index.html">condemned the White House ban</a>. </p>

<p>At the time, Kelly <a href="https://constitutioncenter.org/blog/cnn-gets-temporary-due-process-ruling-in-trump-case">granted CNN a temporary injunction</a> – reinstating Acosta’s press pass. The <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/cnn-drops-suit-against-white-house-after-acostas-press-pass-is-fully-restored/2018/11/19/519763fc-ec3a-11e8-8679-934a2b33be52_story.html">Trump administration later restored Acosta’s credentials</a>, and CNN dropped its lawsuit.</p>

<p>Many commentators and members of the press have called Trump’s latest ban on the three news organizations <a href="https://www.facebook.com/ABCNews/videos/first-amendment-battle-brewing-over-white-house-access/1083884914050614/">a violation of the First Amendment</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760976/original/file-20260920-50-24w631.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A screenshot of a social media post from Donald Trump's account." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760976/original/file-20260920-50-24w631.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760976/original/file-20260920-50-24w631.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=488&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760976/original/file-20260920-50-24w631.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=488&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760976/original/file-20260920-50-24w631.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=488&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760976/original/file-20260920-50-24w631.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=614&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760976/original/file-20260920-50-24w631.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=614&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760976/original/file-20260920-50-24w631.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=614&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">President Donald Trump’s Sept. 18, 2026, social media post announcing he was banning the three news organizations from the White House.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117293599348325006">Truth Social Donald Trump account</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>White House Correspondents’ Association President Jacqui Heinrich said on X that revoking access for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico “<a href="https://x.com/whca/status/2101371576403050530">violates the First Amendment</a>.”</p>

<p>Even George Washington University law professor Jonathan Turley, who staunchly supports Republicans and frequently criticizes the press, said on X that the ban “<a href="https://x.com/JonathanTurley/status/2101041961499058481?s=20">would be an assault on long-honored principles of a free press</a>.” </p>

<p>As Turley and many others have argued, Trump’s ban is almost certainly <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution/first_amendment">unconstitutional under the First Amendment</a>, which states that “Congress shall make no law … abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press.” Media law professor Frank LoMonte argued in 2018, “The First Amendment guarantees all Americans <a href="https://theconversation.com/can-trumps-white-house-legally-ban-reporters-101062">freedom to speak and publish without government interference</a>.” </p>

<p>But they may be missing a crucial point. In fact, there’s more than one constitutional right involved in such a case. Kelly, a Trump appointee, primarily based his 2018 ruling on the reporter’s Fifth Amendment rights to due process, not on the First Amendment. He relied on due process again in ordering access temporarily restored for CNN, MS NOW and Politico.</p>

<p>In my view as a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Q4QLZWEAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">constitutional law professor</a>, it is less clear whether the press has a constitutional right of access to the White House even though past presidents have honored and respected the press’s access to the executive branch. </p>

<p>While several Supreme Court cases, such as <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/448/555/">Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia</a>, unequivocally provide the press with a right of access to criminal trials, there is no Supreme Court precedent that specifically provides a clear constitutional right of access to the White House. </p>



<h2>Make that two constitutional rights</h2>

<p>In one case from 1977, <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/569/124/35083/">Sherrill v. Knight</a>, Robert Sherrill, the Washington correspondent for The Nation, was – after holding press passes over several years – denied a press pass because the Secret Service advised he should not be given one. The Secret Service refused to disclose their justification. </p>

<p>Sherrill sued, and the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals concluded that the Secret Service cannot deny a White House press pass absent “narrow and specific standards by which applications are to be judged.” </p>

<p>The court required the White House to provide the press with “notice of the factual bases for denial, an opportunity for (them) to respond to these, and a final written statement of the reasons for denial (of a press pass).” </p>

<p>In the court’s view, these requirements – notice and an opportunity to rebut the bases for the denial of a press pass – are protected by two constitutional guarantees working together, the press protections in the First Amendment and the <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-5/">Fifth Amendment’s protections</a> from arbitrary deprivations of “life, liberty, or property, without due process of law.” </p>

<p>In other words, before the federal government can deprive an individual of their life, liberty or property, the federal government must provide that individual with <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/due_process">due process</a>, whose purpose is widely accepted as preventing “<a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/due-process-law">arbitrary governmental actions</a>.”</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man in a suit walking near a white building." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=414&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=414&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=414&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=520&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=520&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=520&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta at the White House on Nov. 16, 2018, after a judge ordered his press credential – taken away by President Donald Trump – temporarily restored.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/white-house-correspondent-jim-acosta-arrives-at-the-white-news-photo/1062399128?adppopup=true">Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Due process is key</h2>

<p>There are a number of court decisions relevant to the <a href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754.1.0_1.pdf">journalists’ latest lawsuit</a>, filed Sept. 21, 2026.</p>

<p>Among them is <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/424/319/">Mathews v. Eldridge</a> from 1976, in which the Supreme Court stated that due process is flexible depending on the extent of the liberty or property interest at stake. But in general, the justices said, due process requires the government to provide notice to the individual and an opportunity for the individual to present their case before the deprivation occurs. </p>

<p>In <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/569/124/35083/">Sherrill v. Knight</a> from 1977, the court ruled that the denial of a press pass implicated a First Amendment liberty interest. That interest, the court wrote, “undoubtedly qualifies as liberty which may not be denied without due process of law under the fifth amendment.” </p>

<p>This nuance – the First and Fifth Amendment working in tandem – is what most commentators and critics are missing in their response to the recent ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico. In fact, these outlets collectively lead with their claim that the Trump administration violated their Fifth Amendment right to due process in their <a href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754.1.0_1.pdf">lawsuit to block Trump’s ban</a>.</p>

<p>“Even if attending a White House event is not a constitutionally guaranteed right, that doesn’t mean the government <a href="https://theconversation.com/can-trumps-white-house-legally-ban-reporters-101062">is free to take it away as punishment</a>,” LoMonte argued in 2018.</p>

<p>According to Kelly’s ruling, the Trump administration did not provide CNN, MS NOW or Politico with <a href="https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a0-c343-d2df-a1f4-f7cf04bf0000">written notice stating the reasons for the revocation</a> of their press passes before taking them away. And, in my view, it certainly did not provide the outlets with an opportunity to rebut Trump’s unsupported claim that they report “FICTION and LIES.”</p>

<p><em>This is an updated version of <a href="https://theconversation.com/when-presidents-ban-journalists-from-the-white-house-the-first-amendment-is-not-the-only-constitutional-right-at-stake-292435">an article</a> originally published on Sept. 21, 2026. It was further updated to reflect reporters being allowed back into the White House.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292737/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

As he had in a similar case in 2018 , U.S
District Judge Timothy Kelly decided the revocation of the reporters’ press passes likely violated their Fifth Amendment right to due process

His decision comes just days after President Donald Trump revoked credentials from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, citing “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” On social media, Trump posted, “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President .” This was not Trump’s first attempt at banning journalists from the White House

In that conflict, CNN filed a lawsuit, arguing that, “If left unchallenged, the actions of the White House would create a dangerous chilling effect for any journalist who covers our elected officials .” Journalism organizations also responded
The Committee to Protect Journalists, the Radio Television Digital News Association and even Acosta’s peers at The Daily Caller – a right-leaning news outlet – condemned the White House ban
At the time, Kelly granted CNN a temporary injunction – reinstating Acosta’s press pass
The Trump administration later restored Acosta’s credentials , and CNN dropped its lawsuit
