<title>21 years after disaster helped bring peace to Aceh – has botched Indonesian response to floods reignited calls for independence?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761719/original/file-20260923-50-392hy3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=7%2C0%2C6033%2C4022&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A Free Aceh Movement flag, right, flies alongside the Indonesian national flag during a rally outside the Baiturrahman Grand Mosque in Banda Aceh on Aug. 15, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/man-climbs-a-flagpole-as-he-attempts-to-raise-a-free-aceh-news-photo/2290041204?adppopup=true">Reza Saifullah/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Thousands gathered at Baiturrahman Grand Mosque in Banda Aceh on <a href="https://en.tempo.co/read/2117590/aceh-peace-day-tribute-turns-violent-as-crowd-clashes-with-police">Aug. 15, 2026</a>, to commemorate <a href="https://theacehpost.com/news/bendera-merah-putih-di-pendopo-gubernur-aceh-diturunkan-massa-berkibar-bulan-bintang/index.html">21 years</a> of peace between Indonesia and the separatist Free Aceh Movement, or GAM. </p>

<p>Some participants raised GAM’s red, black and white crescent-star flag and chanted “Free Aceh,” while others lowered Indonesia’s national flag and replaced it with the former separatist movement’s flag. </p>

<p>These were politically significant acts in a province where GAM fought a nearly <a href="https://media.defense.gov/2025/Apr/07/2003683780/-1/-1/0/20250407_INDONESIA_ACEH_1976-2005%20_FINAL.PDF">three-decade</a> armed struggle for independence before the 2005 Helsinki agreement ended the conflict.</p>

<p>And the Aug. 15 display was not an isolated incident. In <a href="https://www.thejakartapost.com/indonesia/2024/12/05/gams-crescent-and-star-flag-raised-in-lhoukseumawe">December 2024</a>, former GAM members raised the crescent-star flag during the movement’s anniversary, with one former combatant expressing hope that it would eventually fly across Aceh. The flag appeared publicly again in <a href="https://en.tempo.co/read/2076220/tni-disperses-crowds-flying-gam-flags-in-acehs-lhokseumawe">December 2025</a>, at which point Indonesian soldiers dispersed crowds displaying it.</p>

<p>The return of these independence symbols and slogans comes as Aceh continues to recover from severe floods and landslides that struck the province in late <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/death-toll-rises-to-164-after-floods-and-landslides-on-indonesias-sumatra-island">November 2025</a>. </p>

<p>A different natural disaster, the 2004 tsunami, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoforum.2007.10.010">helped create conditions</a> that accelerated the peace process between Aceh and Jakarta. Yet two decades later, it is <a href="https://news.mongabay.com/2026/06/survivors-sue-indonesian-government-over-response-to-catastrophic-sumatra-floods/">criticism</a> of the central government’s response to the latest emergency that has served to intensify expressions of independence.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://pol.illinois.edu/directory/profile/astrina2">scholar of nationalism and political geography</a>, I see the resurgence of pro-independence sentiment in Aceh not simply as evidence that separatism is returning, but also as a reminder that national belonging is continually negotiated between states and citizens, and can be harmed by perceived neglect in times of need.</p>

<p><iframe id="30hzF" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/30hzF/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of Indonesia"></iframe></p>

<p>That matters beyond Aceh. The peace agreement transformed a bloody separatist conflict into one of Southeast Asia’s best examples of <a href="https://globalsouthforum.org/article/aceh-at-the-crossroads-hope-for-peace-and-political-challenges-in-a-new-era">post-conflict reconciliation</a>. Renewed tensions would raise questions not only about Aceh’s relationship with Indonesia, but also the durability of a peace settlement that has held for more than two decades.</p>

<h2>Peace ended war, not nationalism</h2>

<p>GAM’s struggle was about more than opposition to policies made in Jakarta. Founded in 1976, the movement presented Aceh — located on the island of Sumatra at the westernmost edge of Indonesia — as a distinct nation that should be independent from Indonesia. GAM drew on Acehnese history to portray independence <a href="https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1469-8129.2007.00277.x">as the restoration</a> of a sovereignty that had existed when Aceh was an independent sultanate. The nearly three-decade conflict <a href="https://reliefweb.int/report/indonesia/no-peace-without-justice-victims-indonesia%E2%80%99s-aceh-conflict-demand-truth-justice-and">killed thousands</a>. Civilians bore much of the violence, with Indonesian security forces and GAM both <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2005/05/27/acehs-forgotten-victims">implicated in abuses</a>, including torture, arbitrary arrests, extortion and forced displacement.</p>

<p>The devastating tsunami of 2004 <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoforum.2007.10.010">acted as a catalyst to peace</a>, shining a light on the suffering of Aceh’s population while opening the doors to international aid and presence.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A boat lies on rubble and debris." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761832/original/file-20260923-50-jorja0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761832/original/file-20260923-50-jorja0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761832/original/file-20260923-50-jorja0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761832/original/file-20260923-50-jorja0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761832/original/file-20260923-50-jorja0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=497&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761832/original/file-20260923-50-jorja0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=497&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761832/original/file-20260923-50-jorja0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=497&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Banda Aceh was one of the hardest-hit regions struck by the 2004 tsunami.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/banda-aceh-after-the-tsunami-disaster-on-january-10-2005-in-news-photo/109132162?adppopup=true">Patrick Aventurier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The armed conflict officially ended with the signing of the <a href="https://peacemaker.un.org/sites/default/files/document/files/2024/05/id050815memorandum20of20understanding.pdf">2005 Helsinki</a> agreement, but it did not make Acehnese nationalism disappear. Instead, it made room for Aceh’s political distinctiveness within Indonesia. The agreement gave Aceh extensive self-governing powers, allowing local political parties, expanding political representation and granting the region the authority to enact provincial laws. Substantial discretion over economic affairs and natural resources was handed to Aceh, although lingering grievances over <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/27638587">revenue-sharing provisions related to the province’s gas fields</a> remain to this day.</p>

<p>The political settlement largely succeeded in ending the organized armed campaign for independence.</p>

<p>GAM disarmed, and many of its former leaders <a href="https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/186810341002900105">moved into</a> electoral politics, forming local parties and winning positions in Aceh’s government and legislature. But while the armed movement ended, pro-independence ideas and symbols did not disappear entirely.</p>

<p>That distinction matters because peace did not depend on Acehnese abandoning their distinct political identity and simply becoming Indonesian; it depended on changing the terms of their relationship with Indonesia. </p>

<p>Aceh could remain part of the country while retaining considerable control over its own political affairs. In that sense, Helsinki did more than end a war. It created political conditions that made remaining within Indonesia acceptable. </p>

<h2>From disaster to independence talk</h2>

<p>The November 2025 floods and landslides killed <a href="https://thediplomat.com/2025/12/acehs-bitter-lesson-relearned/">more than 1,000 people</a> and forced more than 1 million to relocate. Aceh was among the hardest-hit provinces.</p>

<p>It brought citizens into much more direct contact with the Indonesian government and made people dependent on public authorities for assistance and recovery.</p>

<p>Calls for Jakarta to designate the floods and landslides a <a href="https://www.kompas.id/artikel/en-desakan-penetapan-bencana-nasional-di-sumatera-terus-mengalir-dari-aceh">national disaster</a> began soon after they struck, but President Prabowo Subianto rejected them, arguing that Indonesia had sufficient capacity to manage the crisis. Prabowo’s rejection of foreign aid, in particular, led to <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ckgzwqjpzp4o">widespread anger in Aceh</a> and provided a strong contrast to the response in 2004, when international assistance was crucial to the post-tsunami effort.</p>

<p>Almost a year later, significant challenges persist in Aceh. As of Sept. 7, 2026, only <a href="https://www.antaranews.com/berita/5730356/satgas-prr-catat-649-unit-hunian-tetap-di-aceh-telah-rampung">649 of the 34,777 permanent homes</a> needed for those displaced had been completed. The latest available data also showed that 93 regional road segments remained nonfunctional, while only 188 of 676 bridges had been restored as of <a href="https://dialeksis.com/aceh/sembilan-bulan-pascabencana-warga-aceh-masih-menunggu-rumah-dan-akses-permanen/">Aug. 8</a>.</p>

<p>On <a href="https://en.tempo.co/read/2117590/aceh-peace-day-tribute-turns-violent-as-crowd-clashes-with-police">Aug. 14</a> – one day before the GAM flag event – a civil-society coalition again raised white flags and called on Jakarta to declare the disaster a national disaster.</p>

<p>But why do grievances over the government’s response turn into pro-independence talk in Aceh?</p>

<p>History offers part of the answer. A strong Acehnese identity has not always meant wanting to leave Indonesia. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-8129.2007.00277.x">Acehnese leaders</a> supported Indonesian independence from the Dutch colonial empire in 1945, and even the <a href="https://media.defense.gov/2024/Mar/20/2003416575/-1/-1/0/20240306_DARULISLAM_1949-62.PDF">Darul Islam rebellion</a> of the 1950s – which sought to transform Indonesia into an Islamic state – did not seek an independent Acehnese country. Opposition to Dutch colonial rule, followed by Islamic networks and solidarity, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-8129.2007.00277.x">helped connect</a> Acehnese elites to the wider Indonesian political community.</p>

<p>It was only later, as relations with the central government deteriorated, that independence became the goal.</p>

<p>This history suggests that Acehnese nationalism is not a fixed political force that periodically resurfaces unchanged. Different understandings of the nation can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-8129.2007.00277.x">compete and be renegotiated</a> as political conditions change. Acehnese and Indonesian national identities are therefore not necessarily mutually exclusive; their relationship has changed as the political relationship between Aceh and Jakarta has changed.</p>

<p>The return of “Free Aceh” chants and GAM-associated symbols shows that, more than two decades after the peace agreement, independence remains available as a political language for expressing dissatisfaction with Indonesia — especially in moments like natural disasters that have hurt <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111%2Fgove.12440">government legitimacy</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A woman with a megaphone stands in front of posters." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761727/original/file-20260923-50-k9toka.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761727/original/file-20260923-50-k9toka.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761727/original/file-20260923-50-k9toka.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761727/original/file-20260923-50-k9toka.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761727/original/file-20260923-50-k9toka.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761727/original/file-20260923-50-k9toka.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761727/original/file-20260923-50-k9toka.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">An activist in Banda Aceh shouts slogans during a protest over the Indonesian government’s handling of the November 2025 floods.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/an-activist-shouts-slogans-during-a-protest-demanding-the-news-photo/2289880320?adppopup=true">Chaideer Mahyuddin/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Nationalism as a two-way process</h2>

<p>For more than two decades, Aceh has remained peaceful and within Indonesia, while retaining extensive autonomy and a distinct political identity. </p>

<p>Yet the continued use of “Free Aceh” slogans and separatist symbols shows that belonging to Indonesia is not simply settled by peace, autonomy or the passage of time. Nor can nationalism be understood simply by looking at how countries build identity through <a href="https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/nana.70002">schools, maps, flags and ceremonies</a>. </p>

<p>Rather, nationalism works both ways: Indonesia promotes a shared identity, but Acehnese also negotiate what belonging to Indonesia means through their interaction with the state.</p>

<p>Perhaps the more important question, then, is not why independence talk has returned, but what has kept Aceh within Indonesia for the past 21 years.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290480/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Renewed tensions would raise questions not only about Aceh’s relationship with Indonesia, but also the durability of a peace settlement that has held for more than two decades
Peace ended war, not nationalism GAM’s struggle was about more than opposition to policies made in Jakarta
Founded in 1976, the movement presented Aceh — located on the island of Sumatra at the westernmost edge of Indonesia — as a distinct nation that should be independent from Indonesia
GAM drew on Acehnese history to portray independence as the restoration of a sovereignty that had existed when Aceh was an independent sultanate
The nearly three-decade conflict killed thousands
Civilians bore much of the violence, with Indonesian security forces and GAM both implicated in abuses , including torture, arbitrary arrests, extortion and forced displacement
The devastating tsunami of 2004 acted as a catalyst to peace , shining a light on the suffering of Aceh’s population while opening the doors to international aid and presence
Banda Aceh was one of the hardest-hit regions struck by the 2004 tsunami
Patrick Aventurier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images The armed conflict officially ended with the signing of the 2005 Helsinki agreement, but it did not make Acehnese nationalism disappear
Instead, it made room for Aceh’s political distinctiveness within Indonesia
The agreement gave Aceh extensive self-governing powers, allowing local political parties, expanding political representation and granting the region the authority to enact provincial laws

Substantial discretion over economic affairs and natural resources was handed to Aceh, although lingering grievances over revenue-sharing provisions related to the province’s gas fields remain to this day
The political settlement largely succeeded in ending the organized armed campaign for independence
GAM disarmed, and many of its former leaders moved into electoral politics, forming local parties and winning positions in Aceh’s government and legislature
But while the armed movement ended, pro-independence ideas and symbols did not disappear entirely

That distinction matters because peace did not depend on Acehnese abandoning their distinct political identity and simply becoming Indonesian; it depended on changing the terms of their relationship with Indonesia
Aceh could remain part of the country while retaining considerable control over its own political affairs
In that sense, Helsinki did more than end a war
It created political conditions that made remaining within Indonesia acceptable
From disaster to independence talk The November 2025 floods and landslides killed more than 1,000 people and forced more than 1 million to relocate
It brought citizens into much more direct contact with the Indonesian government and made people dependent on public authorities for assistance and recovery

Calls for Jakarta to designate the floods and landslides a national disaster began soon after they struck, but President Prabowo Subianto rejected them, arguing that Indonesia had sufficient capacity to manage the crisis

Prabowo’s rejection of foreign aid, in particular, led to widespread anger in Aceh and provided a strong contrast to the response in 2004, when international assistance was crucial to the post-tsunami effort
Almost a year later, significant challenges persist in Aceh
As of Sept. 7, 2026, only 649 of the 34,777 permanent homes needed for those displaced had been completed
The latest available data also showed that 93 regional road segments remained nonfunctional, while only 188 of 676 bridges had been restored as of Aug. 8
On Aug. 14 – one day before the GAM flag event – a civil-society coalition again raised white flags and called on Jakarta to declare the disaster a national disaster
But why do grievances over the government’s response turn into pro-independence talk in Aceh? History offers part of the answer

<title>Cholesterol control gets personalized – a cardiologist explains how new guidelines tailor treatment to your unique risk profile</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760897/original/file-20260918-50-sjc6cj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5184%2C3456&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Diet is an important lifestyle factor influencing your risk of cardiovascular disease.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/fresh-butter-sliced-on-a-wooden-table-selective-royalty-free-image/1336998559?phrase=cholesterol%20guidelines&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Huizeng Hu/Moment via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>At least a quarter of Americans suffer from high levels of cholesterol or fatty acids in their bloodstream, a condition <a href="https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/hormonal-and-metabolic-disorders/cholesterol-disorders/dyslipidemia">called dyslipidemia</a>. Uncontrolled cholesterol levels increase the risk of <a href="https://www.heart.org/en/professional/quality-improvement/ascvd">atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, or ASCVD</a>: a group of diseases that result from the buildup of plaque in the blood vessels, preventing blood from traveling smoothly to vital organs. This condition can lead to heart attack and stroke.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://www.uchealth.org/provider/william-cornwell-md/">cardiologist with expertise in sports and exercise science</a>, I routinely take care of patients who are interested in making healthy lifestyle choices to control their cholesterol levels, reduce their risk of cardiovascular disease and improve overall health. </p>

<p>In March 2026, new guidelines were provided on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001423">how to treat dyslipidemia</a>, by the American Heart Association and the American College of Cardiology. These guidelines, which were last updated in 2018, include findings from several new studies about how to more effectively treat – and prevent – this condition. </p>

<p>These new guidelines are important for both patients and doctors interested in improving heart health. Of note, these guidelines can help doctors personalize treatment to reduce each individual patient’s risk of developing cardiovascular disease. </p>

<h2>What changed in the new guidelines?</h2>

<p>Compared to prior guidelines, the 2026 update emphasizes the need to treat high cholesterol and fatty acids <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001423">earlier in life and more aggressively</a> in order to reduce the risk of developing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease later in life. </p>

<p>This push toward earlier and more aggressive treatment is based on the observation that there is a strong relationship between the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001303">duration of high cholesterol blood levels and the risk of cardiovascular disease</a> over the span of a lifetime.</p>

<p>The new guidelines provide clinicians with information on how to use <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001423">blood tests and imaging tools</a> to help determine a person’s risk of developing cardiovascular disease.</p>

<p>Some important blood tests include standard lipid tests like levels of LDL (the “bad” cholesterol) and HDL (the “good” cholesterol), but the new guidelines also emphasize the importance of some newer blood tests like lipoprotein A (LpA) and apolipoprotein B (ApoB). The updated guidelines also recommend checking coronary artery calcium (CAC) levels, which older guidelines did not include.   </p>

<p>Importantly, the guidelines encourage providers to use an online calculator called <a href="https://professional.heart.org/en/guidelines-and-statements/prevent-calculator">PREVENT-ASCVD</a>, which uses several factors to determine whether a patient is at low, intermediate or high risk for cardiovascular disease. These factors include body mass index, blood pressure, diabetes history, kidney function and smoking status. The PREVENT-ASCVD calculator also provides an estimate of someone’s risk of cardiovascular disease over 10 years starting at age 30, as well as a risk estimate over the next 30 years.</p>

<p>Based on a patient’s risk level, the guidelines list several newer classes of medications that can be incorporated into a treatment plan for high cholesterol levels. Medications called statins – such as atorvastatin (Lipitor) and rosuvastatin (Crestor) – remain the standard of care for cholesterol management. <a href="https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/cholesterol/prevention-and-treatment-of-high-cholesterol-hyperlipidemia/cholesterol-medications">Several types of additional medications</a> are recommended if statins alone are unable to help patients achieve their cholesterol goals or if a patient experiences intolerable side effects on statins.  </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760901/original/file-20260918-50-2hfu95.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Illustration of a healthy blood vessel on top of a bulging blood vessel with atherosclerosis." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760901/original/file-20260918-50-2hfu95.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760901/original/file-20260918-50-2hfu95.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=375&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760901/original/file-20260918-50-2hfu95.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=375&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760901/original/file-20260918-50-2hfu95.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=375&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760901/original/file-20260918-50-2hfu95.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=471&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760901/original/file-20260918-50-2hfu95.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=471&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760901/original/file-20260918-50-2hfu95.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=471&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Why were the guidelines updated?</h2>

<p>In the mid-20th century, physiologists identified two molecules key to cardiovascular disease: LDL and HDL cholesterol. Epidemiologists observed that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2015.01.036">high LDL was tied to an increase in heart attack risk</a>.  </p>

<p>In the 1980s, two physiologists were awarded the Nobel Prize for <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/ATVBAHA.108.179564">discovering the LDL receptor</a>, a protein on the surface of cells that regulates how much LDL cholesterol is brought into cells. This foundational work transformed the way doctors thought about heart health and cardiovascular disease.  </p>

<p>In the new guidelines, LDL remains the traditional marker for determining cardiovascular disease risk. Other biomarkers like triglycerides and total cholesterol also remain important to check. </p>

<p>However, the guidelines include two newer markers – ApoB and LpA – that may help determine cardiovascular disease risk beyond LDL alone.  </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08223-0">ApoB is a chemical structure</a> that can be found on plaque-forming particles like LDL. While LDL measures the mass of plaques in the blood, ApoB measures the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamacardio.2021.5083">number of plaque particles in the blood</a>. In some scenarios, ApoB may more accurately predict someone’s risk of cardiovascular disease than LDL cholesterol, especially for patients with diabetes or <a href="https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/metabolic-syndrome/about-metabolic-syndrome">metabolic syndrome</a>. It can also be particularly useful for patients who have normal LDL levels but elevated levels of other lab values like triglycerides.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01308-4">LpA is a molecule</a> similar to LDL cholesterol in structure, but with an extra protein attached to it called <a href="https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/lipoprotein-a-blood-test/">apolipoprotein A</a>. This protein is stickier and more prone to cause plaque or blockages in arteries than LDL alone. Elevated levels of LpA may increase a person’s lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease; the higher the LpA level, the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001423">higher the risk of cardiovascular disease</a>. The guidelines recommend checking LpA once in all adults to help determine their lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease.    </p>

<p>Finally, the new guidelines also provide information on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy217">coronary artery calcium scores</a>. Obtained from a CT scan, these scores directly measure the amount of calcium deposits in the arteries around the heart. The greater the amount of calcium, the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy217">greater the risk of cardiovascular disease</a>. The guidelines provide specific recommendations for managing cholesterol levels depending on the amount of calcium in a patient’s arteries.  </p>

<p>These patient-specific targets are representative of the broader goal of the new guidelines – namely, to personalize treatment plans based on each patient’s unique risk profile.</p>

<h2>How do the new guidelines affect treatment?</h2>

<p>The new guidelines shift how doctors manage cholesterol levels toward earlier screening and more personalized treatment. They emphasize the importance of lifelong prevention strategies to reduce risk of cardiovascular disease. </p>

<p>The guidelines recommend <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001423">checking lipid levels very early in life</a>. Children ages 9 to 11 should have their cholesterol levels checked to identify any lipid abnormalities. Starting at age 19, adults should have cholesterol levels checked every five years. Adults at an increased risk of cardiovascular disease may also consider starting medications at age 30. </p>

<p>The guidelines also recommend what’s called a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001423">CPR model</a> of cholesterol management: </p>

<ul>
<li><p>Calculate the patient’s 10-year cardiovascular disease risk. </p></li>
<li><p>Personalize their estimated risk by considering other factors like family history, blood test results and existing conditions. </p></li>
<li><p>Reclassify patients with additional imaging scans. </p></li>
<li><p>Reassess treatment recommendations based on this information.</p></li>
</ul>

<p>This approach underscores the importance of personalizing treatment decisions based on each individual patient’s risk. </p>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/group-of-healthy-ingredients-high-in-unsaturated-royalty-free-image/2251587005?phrase=cholesterol%20guidelines&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">fcafotodigital/iStock via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What do the guidelines say about lifestyle?</h2>

<p>It is important to remember that healthy lifestyle choices remain the foundation for preventing cardiovascular disease.    </p>

<p>The American Heart Association recommends specific healthy behaviors it calls <a href="https://www.heart.org/en/healthy-living/healthy-lifestyle/lifes-essential-8">Life’s Essential 8</a> to help reduce cardiovascular disease risk. These include getting enough sleep, quitting tobacco and managing blood pressure, among others.</p>

<p>The new cholesterol guidelines emphasize the importance of modifying diet, including reducing the amount of sugar, refined carbohydrates, saturated fats and alcohol a person consumes each day.</p>

<p>The guidelines emphasize the importance of routine exercise. Specifically, they recommend 150 minutes per week of moderate intensity exercise, or 75 minutes per week of vigorous exercise throughout adulthood. They also recommend two days per week of resistance exercise.</p>

<p>Lastly, the guidelines recommend weight loss of around 5% to 10% of total body weight for patients who are overweight or obese to help reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/279080/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>AI tools can help Americans meet their civil legal needs</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760571/original/file-20260917-70-rnft5s.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=157%2C0%2C6001%2C4000&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Civil defendants in the U.S. have no constitutional right to an attorney, unlike defendants in criminal cases.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/laws-and-regulations-concept-man-touches-digital-royalty-free-image/2187645582?phrase=AI%20legal%20services&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">iStock/Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Most Americans know that in all criminal cases – those filed by the government against an accused individual – the defendant has <a href="https://www.nacdl.org/Landing/Right-to-Counsel">a constitutional right to a lawyer</a>. The Supreme Court established this right in 1963 in the landmark case <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1962/155">Gideon v. Wainright</a>.</p>

<p>What many people may not know is that <a href="https://www.americanbar.org/groups/legal_aid_indigent_defense/civil_right_to_counsel1/">no such right exists in civil cases</a>. Civil cases are those filed by individuals or businesses against other individuals or businesses – for example, a landlord against a tenant, a bank against a borrower or an employee against an employer. These cases affect rights that many Americans take for granted, including housing, healthcare and education.</p>

<p>But calls for a civil right to counsel, or “<a href="https://www.americanbar.org/groups/legal_aid_indigent_defense/civil_right_to_counsel1/">civil Gideon</a>,” have gone unanswered for years. Meanwhile, the United States <a href="https://civilrighttocounsel.org/major_developments/u-s-rank-on-access-to-civil-justice-in-rule-of-law-index-116th-out-of-142-countries/">ranks 112th of 143 countries</a> on access and affordability to civil legal services. This is 40 spots lower than a decade ago, <a href="https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/administrative/news/2025/2025-natl-lawyer-population-survey.pdf">despite a 6% increase</a> in the U.S. practicing lawyer population during the same period.</p>

<h2>Access to justice</h2>

<p>Studies show that low-income Americans receive insufficient or no legal help for <a href="https://justicegap.lsc.gov/">92% of their civil legal problems</a>.
Nonprofit legal aid organizations fill some of this “justice gap.” </p>

<p>However, <a href="https://justicegap.lsc.gov/resource/executive-summary/">49% of those whose income is low enough</a> to qualify for services are turned away because <a href="https://evictionlab.org/legal-aid-under-threat/">legal services organizations lack resources</a>. The number of people turned away does not include those who <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/01/26/2026-01431/income-level-for-individuals-eligible-for-assistance">make too much money to qualify</a> for legal aid, typically 125% of the federal poverty level, <a href="https://www.healthcare.gov/glossary/federal-poverty-level-fpl/">or US$37,878 for a family of four</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://directory.law.wfu.edu/murphyme/">My scholarship</a>, along with that of others, suggest that the U.S. cannot lawyer itself out of this crisis. The legal system has failed to provide the resources that these seniors, veterans, children, rural Americans and others need to defend their legal rights or even understand their legal problems. </p>

<p>I believe the proliferation of AI-powered chatbots and legal services offers a new means of addressing these unmet legal needs.</p>

<h2>AI legal services</h2>

<p>Since ChatGPT’s release in November 2022, concerns over lawyers’ sloppy AI use <a href="https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en/institute/articles/genai-hallucinations">have dominated headlines</a>, including instances where attorneys have cited <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/09/us/ai-lawyers-sanctioned-mississippi.html">fake legal cases in court filings</a>.</p>

<p>Typically overlooked is how AI has changed the way ordinary people interact with the law. AI offers not only ready access to free legal information that was <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2942478">once hard to find</a>, but also customized solutions to legal problems.</p>

<p>Two types of AI tools are relevant. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760573/original/file-20260917-50-pb6cax.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman types on a laptop while seated at a desk." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760573/original/file-20260917-50-pb6cax.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760573/original/file-20260917-50-pb6cax.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760573/original/file-20260917-50-pb6cax.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760573/original/file-20260917-50-pb6cax.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760573/original/file-20260917-50-pb6cax.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760573/original/file-20260917-50-pb6cax.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760573/original/file-20260917-50-pb6cax.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Low-income Americans receive insufficient or no legal help for 92% of their civil legal problems.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/hologram-and-the-woman-using-a-laptop-computer-the-royalty-free-image/2006713125?phrase=AI%20legal%20services&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Narumon Bowonkitwanchai/Moment via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The first type is widely known and broadly available: the multipurpose AI platforms like ChatGPT and Claude. Built on massive datasets of information, these tools provide unrestricted, easy access to legal information and resources. They can also provide tailored answers to specific questions, including legal ones.</p>

<p>The second type is less well known. Niche AI tools are built on information relevant to a specific domain, like law. These types of tools are designed to understand the nuance of a field and assist with a narrow task. For example, <a href="https://legalaidnc.org/lia/">Legal Aid of North Carolina offers a self-service AI</a> tool that can answer users’ specific legal questions about child custody, domestic violence or consumer law.</p>

<p>Both multipurpose and niche tools can provide generic legal information as well as advice about a person’s legal problem. However, <a href="https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/domain-specific-llm">niche AIs are more accurate</a> because they are trained on legal rather than generalized data and, therefore, they are more precise and relevant.</p>

<p>Nonetheless, <a href="https://www.law360.com/pulse/articles/2512858">multipurpose tools have proven skilled</a> at helping litigants without access to lawyers. <a href="https://www.law360.com/pulse/articles/2512858">Early data</a> indicate that these self-represented people are filing more cases as ChatGPT and similar tools became available. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/06/04/1138391/courts-coping-ai-lawsuits/">Judges agree</a> that the increase in self-represented litigants may be attributable to AI. However, access to the courts has not yet resulted in <a href="https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/06/04/1138391/courts-coping-ai-lawsuits/">better chances of winning one’s lawsuit</a>.</p>

<h2>Pros and cons of AI use</h2>

<p>Opponents of self-represented litigants have complained about the proliferation of cases and <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/25/us/politics/artificial-intelliegence-courts.html">improper filings created by multipurpose AI</a>. Judges have expressed frustration with self-represented parties dumping “<a href="https://www.law360.com/pulse/articles/2512858">hundreds of pages of documents</a>” on the court. </p>

<p>Furthermore, without individualized human interaction, algorithmic-driven legal advice could harm litigants who are most in need of help by providing erroneous or incomplete advice.</p>

<p>Both <a href="https://natlawreview.com/article/case-was-settled-chatgpt-thought-otherwise-dispute-poised-define-ai-legal-liability">multipurpose</a> and <a href="https://www.floridabar.org/the-florida-bar-news/tikds-online-service-found-to-be-upl/">niche legal tools</a> are plagued by the legal profession’s self-imposed limits on who can deliver legal services. When individuals other than lawyers provide legal advice or otherwise engage in the practice of law, it is known as the <a href="https://www.westacademic.com/The-Unauthorized-Practice-of-Law-An-Interactive-Course-Concise-Video-Edition-3">unauthorized practice of law</a>, or UPL. UPL restrictions are designed to ensure the public receives competent and ethical legal representation. </p>

<p>However, AI offers those who may not even understand they have a legal problem an opportunity to access information and assistance. AI can help people without counsel better understand the merits of their case and perhaps even <a href="https://www.abajournal.com/web/article/Tell-me-how-to-get-even-with-my-lawyer?">understand the court procedure</a> necessary to successfully represent themselves.</p>

<p>These tools are not without risk. But, without them, we may continue to meet only 8% percent of the civil legal needs of Americans. Everyone else will continue to do without.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290772/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>ICE arrests at Philadelphia International evoke time when airport police helped military catch AWOL Vietnam War soldiers in 1960s</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761528/original/file-20260922-50-itb1gv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8256%2C5504&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">ICE increased its presence at more than a dozen U.S. airports in 2026, including Philadelphia International Airport.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/an-ice-agent-stands-alongside-a-long-line-of-travelers-news-photo/2268242754">Matthew Hatcher/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>ICE ramped up its <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/26/record-arrests-deportations-immigrants">arrests of immigrants</a> at major airports over the summer of 2026, <a href="https://whyy.org/articles/ice-agents-philadelphia-airport/">including in Philadelphia</a>, to help meet the Trump administration’s reported goal of <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/01/us/politics/ice-immigrant-arrests-surge.html">apprehending 1,100 people daily</a>. </p>

<p>The agency is collaborating with the Transportation Security Administration, its sister agency in the Department of Homeland Security. However, decades before TSA existed, <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691238838/police-against-the-movement">local police were used in a similar fashion</a> to help the military catch AWOL Vietnam War soldiers.</p>

<p>I’m a <a href="https://nyupress.org/9781479823987/hope-and-struggle-in-the-policed-city/">historian of race and policing in Philadelphia</a> after the Civil Rights Movement and I spend a lot of time digging through the <a href="https://www.phila.gov/departments/department-of-records/city-archives/">city’s archives</a>. I recently combed through a 1967 collection of police incident reports from the 77th district, also known as the airport police, which patrols <a href="https://www.phl.org/about/history">Philadelphia International Airport</a>.</p>

<p>Most of the cases involved plane crashes and unruly passengers, rental car thefts, larceny of luggage and freight packages, bomb scares and drug smuggling.</p>

<p>But the airport police at times detained <a href="https://scholarshare.temple.edu/items/c3c405e6-129e-4074-bf2d-72b2c1384636">drafted soldiers</a> who didn’t want to complete their tours of duty.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761559/original/file-20260922-60-xexrqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Black and white photo of street scene with billboard encouraging men to sign up for Army and anti-war graffiti on the billboard" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761559/original/file-20260922-60-xexrqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761559/original/file-20260922-60-xexrqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=812&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761559/original/file-20260922-60-xexrqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=812&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761559/original/file-20260922-60-xexrqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=812&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761559/original/file-20260922-60-xexrqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1020&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761559/original/file-20260922-60-xexrqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1020&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761559/original/file-20260922-60-xexrqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1020&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A site of civil disobedience</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://digital.library.temple.edu/digital/collection/p15037coll3/id/22298/rec/3">Vietnam War was unpopular</a> because the goals of America’s <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt36242714">fight against communism</a> were unclear and <a href="https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/vietnam-my-lai-massacre/">village massacres like My Lai</a> exposed it as unjust. </p>

<p>Approximately <a href="https://uncpress.org/9780807843918/working-class-war/">80% of American soldiers</a> drafted were working-class men. The odds of facing <a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/Handbook_of_Aging_and_the_Social_Science/xNTUBQAAQBAJ?hl=en&amp;gbpv=0">injury, amputation, post-traumatic stress disorder and death</a> in this war were higher than that of World War II and the Korean War.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.archives.gov/research/military/vietnam-war/casualty-statistics">Nearly 60,000</a> U.S. military personnel lost their lives during the Vietnam War. The death toll was at its highest between 1967 and 1969, when at least 11,000 U.S. troops died each year.</p>

<p><a href="https://philadelphiaencyclopedia.org/essays/vietnam-war/">One in five Pennsylvanians who died in the war</a> were from Philadelphia. Edison High School in North Philadelphia had the <a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/Edison_64/UClWEQAAQBAJ?hl=en&amp;gbpv=0">greatest number of high school students killed in Vietnam</a> nationwide: 64.</p>

<p>In 1967, Philadelphia’s local police functioned as the federal government’s eyes and ears to report anti-war behavior at the airport.</p>

<p>That February,  and questioned <a href="https://www.newspapers.com/article/delaware-county-daily-times/206317732/">Fred Batchelder</a>, the president of Ridley Park’s <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/community.28445766">Veterans for Peace in Vietnam</a>, for distributing anti-war pamphlets to servicemen without getting authorization from the Division of Aviation. The pamphlets aimed to bust myths about the war and were written by
<a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/07/us/donald-w-duncan-79-ex-green-beret-and-early-critic-of-vietnam-war-is-dead.html">Green Beret Master Sgt. Donald Duncan</a>, an early critic of the war.</p>

<p>Four hours later, Batchelder was released and permitted to distribute pamphlets outside the terminal and in the baggage room. But  to Philadelphia’s Civil Disobedience Squad and the FBI so those agencies could further investigate him.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">

Duncan Tells the Truth' attached on top" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761590/original/file-20260922-50-gaw08o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761590/original/file-20260922-50-gaw08o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761590/original/file-20260922-50-gaw08o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761590/original/file-20260922-50-gaw08o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761590/original/file-20260922-50-gaw08o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761590/original/file-20260922-50-gaw08o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761590/original/file-20260922-50-gaw08o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

<h2>Escapes from military custody</h2>

<p>As Batchelder protested with literature, AWOL soldiers took advantage of the airport’s busy environment to escape from the military police. </p>

<p>The same month that Batchelder was detained, serviceman D. Green, a sailor already under <a href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title10/pdf/USCODE-2024-title10-subtitleA-partII-chap47-subchapX-sec883.pdf">disciplinary action</a> who was being escorted to his ship in San Diego, ran through the main terminal while a shore patrolman from the Navy Yard pursued him.</p>

<p>Airport police joined the chase that led to an undeveloped section of highway nearby. Both law enforcement agencies hailed taxis to follow Green until he was eventually caught, handcuffed and detained. </p>

<p>A few weeks later, Pvt. T.J. Kee escaped the custody of military police escorting him to Baltimore. Once Kee fled from the Delta Airlines ticket counter, Philadelphia and Tinicum township police were alerted to patrol the airport and the surrounding area, but Kee got away. He enjoyed nearly five months of freedom until <a href="https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-philadelphia-inquirer/206464579/4">Delaware state police caught him</a> in Wilmington.</p>

<h2>Soldiers in distress</h2>

<p>Servicemen also used medical emergencies to avoid active duty.</p>

<p>In May 1967, Navy officer P. Nahmens fell ill in the baggage claim area of Philadelphia’s airport and asked police to take him to the Naval Hospital. Nahmens complained that for two months he had severe chest pains and an upset stomach before his return to duty aboard the USS Newman K. Perry in Newport, Rhode Island. </p>

<p>Nahmens also said that he did not want to report to his superiors, which I believe made the police suspicious because they used the uncommon classification, “ill sailor” in their files to document the incident.</p>

<p>That same month, Pvt. Wishler had a seizure in the airport’s baggage room after he arrived from Phoenix on a TWA flight. Wishler was scheduled to report to Fort Dix in New Jersey within seven hours of landing in Philadelphia. Airport police attended to him, but it appears from their report that they weren’t fully convinced he was actually unconscious and having convulsions. </p>

<p>Skycap Ben Austin, who assisted passengers with picking up their luggage, reported the emergency and another soldier told the police he witnessed Wishler shaking and saw saliva dripping from his mouth. However, after Officer R.A. D'Ambrosio saw Wishler, he stated in his signed incident report that the serviceman only “appeared” to be unconscious and convulsing.</p>

<p>Wishler was transported to the Naval Hospital, and the police later called the hospital to investigate his medical condition. They closed the case after they learned Wishler had fractured his skull in a prior accident that made him prone to seizures.</p>

<p>Dying by suicide was another option servicemen considered.</p>

<p>In July 1967, Army Officer J. Fries told his sergeant that he was “afraid to go to Viet Nam and was going to end it all.” He later survived an overdose of aspirin in a Philadelphia airport restroom. Airport attendant Marie Jones found the unconscious soldier and informed the police, who later transported him to the Naval Hospital for a stomach pump.</p>

          </figure>

<h2>Protesters demand ICE leave PHL</h2>

<p>In the decades that followed, local police continued to assist the federal government with national security and surveillance at Philadelphia’s airport until TSA was established in 2001 in the wake of the <a href="https://www.911memorial.org/">September 11 attacks</a> by the militant group al-Qaida. </p>

<p>During the spring and summer of 2026, peaceful protesters often gathered outside terminals at Philadelphia International to <a href="https://templeupdate.com/ice-presence-at-phl-airport/">demand that ICE stop intimidating travelers</a> and leave the airport. <a href="https://northeasttimes.com/2026/08/01/ice-arrests-at-least-seven-people-at-philadelphia-airport-since-mid-july/">Immigration advocates</a> from <a href="https://www.aaunited.org/">Asian Americans United</a> have documented <a href="https://www.inquirer.com/news/airport-arrests-ice-trump-philadelphia-international-airport-20260807.html">at least 10 immigrants arrested by ICE</a> at Philadelphia International Airport since July 2026. </p>

<p>Nationwide, <a href="https://www.dhs.gov/cbphome">ICE has encouraged</a> immigrants to <a href="https://www.themarshallproject.org/2025/06/14/ice-immigration-dhs-deportation-facts">self-deport</a> with stipends, free travel and fine forgiveness, or face <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ice-deportations-afghanistan-cuba-africa/">third country deportation</a> and possible incarceration in Latin America or Africa. </p>

<p>Philadelphia’s airport – and airports in cities around the country – remains a frontier for both freedom and apprehension. </p>

<title>Friendship is built over time, through ordinary moments – I teach lonely college students to notice them</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761751/original/file-20260923-50-26k632.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7499%2C5000&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Nearly 6 in 10 college students said in 2026 that they felt lonely sometimes or always. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/people-with-digital-addiction-are-sitting-in-royalty-free-illustration/2056364426?phrase=college%20loneliness&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Denis Novikov/iStock/Getty Images Plus </a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The first skill I learned when <a href="https://www.coastal.edu/academics/facultyprofiles/educationandsocialsciences/politics/justinvaughn/">I became a political science professor</a> nearly 20 years ago was how to quiet a room full of chatty undergraduates. </p>

<p>These days, I often walk into a silent room, with students staring at their phones and barely acknowledging the classmates beside them. </p>

<p>As I read more about the United States’ <a href="https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf">loneliness crisis</a>, I began noticing a version of it among my students. </p>

<p>In a 2026 <a href="https://www.trellisstrategies.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Research-Brief_TSFEB26_Loneliness.pdf">national survey of over 40,000 college students</a>, nearly 6 in 10 said they felt lonely sometimes or always. At the same time, <a href="https://www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/atus.pdf">federal time-use data</a> show that the share of Americans who socialized in person with family, friends or others on an average day fell from 38% in 2015 to 30% in 2025.</p>

<p>Those and <a href="https://www.coastal.edu/honorscollege/centerforappliedcivicleadership/friendship/">similar other studies</a> capture a familiar contradiction seen on college campuses like my own: Many new students want close relationships, but feel anxious about initiating them and have had little practice sustaining them. </p>

<p>I realized that my students rarely spoke to one another, and went entire semesters without learning their classmates’ names. Many students seemed unsure how to cross the few feet between them and their peers and make the social connection they craved.</p>

<p>I <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/why-friendship-belongs-college-classroom-justin-vaughn-ycbme?trk=public_post_feed-article-content">designed a freshman honors seminar</a>, “Friendship &amp; Society,” around this uncertainty, combining the academic study of friendship with practical exercises in forming and sustaining it. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761760/original/file-20260923-50-fqj5ei.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two women walk closely together down a stone path with red brick pillars on either side of them." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761760/original/file-20260923-50-fqj5ei.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761760/original/file-20260923-50-fqj5ei.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761760/original/file-20260923-50-fqj5ei.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761760/original/file-20260923-50-fqj5ei.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761760/original/file-20260923-50-fqj5ei.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761760/original/file-20260923-50-fqj5ei.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761760/original/file-20260923-50-fqj5ei.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">College students in this class learn about how positive social interactions activate the brain’s reward system while isolation triggers a stress response.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/rear-view-of-teenage-female-friends-walking-arm-in-royalty-free-image/2148729634?phrase=college%20friendship&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Klaus Vedfelt/Digital Vision via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Understanding friendship</h2>

<p>In this course, students examine how an <a href="https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/platonic-love/202604/how-to-talk-to-strangers">initial exchange can develop</a> into friendship through <a href="https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/brain-waves/201803/how-do-you-make-or-maintain-friends-put-in-the-time">repeated contact and shared time</a>, and why many potential connections never progress into a lasting friendship.</p>

<p>They consider how friends help shape identity and memory, whether old friends are owed continued loyalty after their lives diverge and whether a friendship can remain meaningful after it ends. </p>

<p>Students also look at how friendship can have strong effects on physical and mental health, making it what I believe is an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/23727322251404386">overlooked public health issue</a>. Friendships can also help shape people’s broader sense of belonging in a community, building the social trust that <a href="https://www.abigailadamsinstitute.org/seeking-the-good-american-democracys-forgotten-institution">civic life depends on</a>.</p>

<p>Students test those questions through 10 “Friendship Practices,” a series of experiential activities I designed. Students are asked to share a meal with classmates or visit a public gathering place like a café or lounge to see how these settings can encourage conversation. During a “friendship safari,” small groups walk across campus, noting where conversations begin and where students pass one another without speaking.</p>

<p>In private journal entries and submitted reflections, students record what they expected from each situation, and what happened when they tried to form connections. They make a short film telling a story of friendship on campus and end with a friendship memoir tracing how their own relationships and expectations changed during their first semester of college.</p>

<h2>Diving into friendship</h2>

<p>Students read “<a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/688054/stay-true-by-hua-hsu/">Stay True</a>,” a memoir about a friendship between author Hsu Hsu and his classmate Ken that shapes Hsu’s sense of himself long after his friend’s death.</p>

<p>Neuroscientist Ben Rein’s book “<a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/761227/why-brains-need-friends-by-ben-rein-phd/">Why Brains Need Friends</a>” explains the biology of connection and isolation, and shows how positive interactions activate the brain’s reward system while isolation triggers a stress response. </p>

<p>Students also read <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2025/02/american-loneliness-personality-politics/681091/">longform journalism</a>, <a href="https://www.coastal.edu/honorscollege/centerforappliedcivicleadership/friendship/">social science research</a>, <a href="https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf">public health reports</a> and <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/T/bo3636037.html">political philosophy</a> on aspects of loneliness. They also watch <a href="https://www.ted.com/talks/kio_stark_why_you_should_talk_to_strangers">TED Talks</a> and <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0374900/">films that explore how a brief encounter</a> with a stranger can, over time, become a friendship. </p>

<h2>Lessons learned</h2>

<p>Students learn that a friendship is built from countless moments that may feel meaningless while they are happening. An unremarkable meal, or a conversation that fills 10 spare minutes rarely feels consequential on its own. </p>

<p>Over time, those moments build relational capital, meaning the shared trust and history friends can draw on when life becomes difficult or a disagreement needs repairing. </p>

<p>That reserve reaches beyond a single relationship. Communities become more connected when people have accumulated enough ordinary experience together to trust one another and keep showing up.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761761/original/file-20260923-50-qfzmnl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Four young women smile and pose as they lift one of the women, wearing a black graduation gown and carrying flowers, in the air." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761761/original/file-20260923-50-qfzmnl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761761/original/file-20260923-50-qfzmnl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=414&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761761/original/file-20260923-50-qfzmnl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=414&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761761/original/file-20260923-50-qfzmnl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=414&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761761/original/file-20260923-50-qfzmnl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=521&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761761/original/file-20260923-50-qfzmnl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=521&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761761/original/file-20260923-50-qfzmnl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=521&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Individual, ordinary moments with peers over time can build and help form a friendship.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/irvine-ca-graduate-abigail-yoo-is-lifted-off-the-ground-by-news-photo/2280602266?adppopup=true">Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>By the end of the course, students can weigh different kinds of evidence about how friendships form, develop and sometimes fade. They also become better able to start a conversation, recognize which public spaces make it easier to meet and spend time with others, and identify habits that help relationships deepen over time.</p>

<p>They finish with a clearer sense of how relationships take shape and how their own choices contribute to the communities forming around them.</p>

title: There’s a global plan to save humans from AI. Can it actually work?
excerpt: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman looks on during a UN Security Council meeting on artificial intelligence during the 81st United Nations General Assembly on September 23,
body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman looks on during a UN Security Council meeting on artificial intelligence during the 81st United Nations General Assembly on September 23, 2026. | Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images When the AI apocalypse becomes regular dinner-table conversation, you know we’ve reached the freakout stage
Rogue AI agents are hacking into competitors
Former Big Tech employees are posting Skynet-style warnings on social media
CEOs are crying for help in ways that have made this once-wonky tech issue a frontline political fight
I still think many of the concerns outlined by the AI leaders themselves are massively self-serving — especially when their companies are soon to go public
But the growing list of AI scandals is real
And it tells us that the status quo for regulating this powerful new technology is not working

The question now on everyone’s mind: Is any kind of global brake possible? What form of AI safety regime is practical, over the short term, when there is no trust between major governments? And what could possibly work when companies are loath to give up their secret sauce and are bent on domination in the global AI race? Two major conversations are now playing out, in real time
On Wednesday, President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington for a three-day summit — part of which will be dedicated to AI risks

The same day, with the United Nations meeting for its annual General Assembly, heads of the world’s leading AI companies urged the UN to police the emerging technology, or risk potentially wiping out humanity. “We could lose control of the future to AI,” OpenAI’s boss, Sam Altman, bluntly told the UN’s Security Council

Confronted with this collective freakout, it’s time to take a long, deep breath.  In fact, AI safety has been on a lot of policymakers’ minds for years now, gaining momentum after ChatGPT was introduced in 2022
Governments have held hearings, convened expert groups, and drafted their own outlines of how to keep it under control
These weren’t just idle listening exercises
They aren’t all well known to the wider public, but they yielded real plans
Barring any breakthroughs this week, we already have a quasi-planetary shield against the potentially runaway technology
The bad news is that it’s not really up and running yet
It’s also not clear whether it will actually work

So what is it — and how can we fix it so we have a global system that responds in time to deal with the incredibly fast-moving threats from AI? What the global AI patchwork looks like now For the last four years, the most tech-savvy nations — and would-be AI leaders — have been running serious conversations about this exact AI safety threat
Some are in Congress and the White House; some at the UN, at the G7, and in other capitals
I’ve been covering this closely as a global technology journalist, from my current perch at a think tank

Here’s what the landscape looks like: There are national AI safety and security institutes , government-funded bodies whose job it is to kick the tires of AI companies’ latest products before they are let loose into the wild

There are also voluntary commitments by companies, many of which have made their own pledges or developed joint standards, to protect elections from AI threats, stop the spread of AI-fueled deepfake imagery, and joint government-corporate efforts to bake safety into how the technology develops

At the international level, there’s a G7-led reporting mechanism — embraced by the most important Western tech nations that allows AI giants to share how they are building their latest models, as well as create standards for how to reduce catastrophic risks
An international scientific report provides a yearly update on risks posed by the most advanced AI systems, based on existing research, to help governments plan for the worst

What’s missing from all that?  What we currently lack — and what is needed between now and the end of 2026 — is a way to turn this cottage industry of AI safety mechanisms into a functioning, but crude, first-responder system when things suddenly go wrong.  The last four years have laid out a pathway, and some of the necessary systems even exist
But there’s no way to respond globally, and in real time, when an AI crisis hits — especially if such a possibly doomsday event cuts across countries already skeptical of each other
This week’s US-China summit may be a step in the right direction

Under proposals outlined by American officials, Washington and Beijing could set up a hotline between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in case of an AI incident affected each country’s national security.  It’s still unclear if Trump’s meeting with Xi will lead to such progress
Chinese officials also have balked at Washington’s pleas for AI rules because, so far, Congress has failed to act, and China already has some of the world’s most stringent AI oversight
For AI to be “safe,” this conversation will need to go beyond this week’s US-China summit
Relying just on Washington and Beijing — arguably the most important AI powers — would not solve the underlying problems, nor would it make other countries feel more comfortable
What we need next, so it really saves us I’ve been talking to AI safety experts and government officials, and it’s clear the missing piece is a way to activate this whole system in a crisis
Countries don’t all have to have the same AI safety policies, and they never will

But as with nuclear weapons — a similarly high-threat technology that the world found a way to contain — safety requires a rough global agreement on how to respond quickly when something goes terribly wrong
What’s needed right now is a 90-day, opt-in rapid response mechanism that joins existing pieces of the AI safety puzzle together
I’ve pieced together some ideas about how it should work, and who needs to sign on
Granted, none of what I outline below is sufficient

But, together, they are more plausible than trying to negotiate a comprehensive global regime — let alone arrange another AI summit — while Washington, Beijing, and other national capitals disagree over what “AI safety” actually means

All of these options are based on existing mechanisms, are derived from efforts that have worked in other policy areas, and provide a band-aid to the AI safety dilemma until a more durable solution can be negotiated
First, developers, AI safety institutes, and regulators, from across different countries, should agree that when an incident occurs, it triggers a specific Chernobyl-style protocol

Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on September 21, 2026. | Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: The media outlets President Donald Trump banned from the White House last week are back.  What happened? Early on Thursday morning, a federal district court ruled that the White House had to immediately restore press credentials for CNN, Politico, and MS NOW and allow the outlets’ reporters back into the building.  The White House did, eventually — but only after multiple reporters were rebuffed over the course of the morning
They were allowed back in around noon, nearly 11 hours after the court’s order
What’s the context? Trump announced the short-lived ban last week on Friday afternoon, writing that outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES” while covering him

He also threatened that additional outlets could be added to the ban.  Why did Trump want to ban journalists in the first place? Most recently, the White House line has been “national security”: On Monday, Trump accused reporters of “violat[ing] our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources.’”  On Thursday, however, Judge Timothy Kelly, a first-term Trump appointee, wrote that the White House offered “little to back up their asserted national security interest.” (According to the media newsletter Status, one of the “unknown sources” the White House was complaining about was none other than Vice President JD Vance , speaking to reporters on a press call.) Trump himself has also suggested a simpler motive: Last week, he told reporters that “it’s really just cumulative stories of the last two years
You get sick of it.” Is this the end of the case? Not yet
Thursday’s ruling was only a temporary restraining order, good for 14 days max, and Kelly has said that he “intends to rule expeditiously” on a more durable preliminary injunction
Trump has already promised to appeal in the extremely likely outcome that the ruling also goes against him

And with that, it’s time to log off… I found this Washington Post article breaking down whether you should get a Covid booster shot this fall extremely useful, and you might too.  Plus: Fat Bear Week is on, and it’s not too late to vote
